nameStory: The Hickory Tussock Moth gets its name from its caterpillar's preferred dining spots – hickory trees – and the fuzzy "tussocks" or clumps of hairs that cover the caterpillar like a punk rock hairdo. While the adult moth is rather plain, it's the dramatically hairy caterpillar that most people encounter and remember, earning this species its memorable moniker.
description: The Hickory Tussock Moth is a medium-sized moth in the tiger moth family, though the adult is much less flashy than its famous fuzzy caterpillar. The adult moth has a wingspan of about 1.5-2 inches with cream-colored wings marked by small dark spots. Most people encounter this species as a caterpillar – a striking white and black fuzzy creature covered in dense tufts of hair that feeds on hickory, walnut, and other hardwood trees. The caterpillar is far more noticeable than the adult moth, which is active at night and attracted to lights.

idTips.label: Fuzzy white caterpillar
idTips.description: The most recognizable stage: a densely hairy white caterpillar with black tufts along the back and longer black pencils of hair at both ends. The hairs feel soft but can cause skin irritation – look but don't touch!

idTips.label: Adult wing pattern
idTips.description: Cream or pale yellow wings with scattered small dark brown or black spots, giving a lightly speckled appearance. Wings feel papery and delicate when found.

idTips.label: Host plant preference
idTips.description: Look for caterpillars on hickory, walnut, butternut, and occasionally oak, elm, or willow trees. They often feed in groups when young, creating visible defoliation.

idTips.label: Caterpillar size and shape
idTips.description: Mature caterpillars reach about 1.5 inches long with a cylindrical body that's completely obscured by dense white hairs. The hair tufts make them appear almost round in cross-section.

idTips.label: Black hair pencils
idTips.description: Distinctive long black hair tufts (called pencils) project from the front and rear of the caterpillar like antennae or a tail. These are longer and more prominent than the body hairs.

habitat: Found throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests where hickory, walnut, and other preferred host trees grow. Most common in lower elevation woodlands, forest edges, and suburban areas with mature shade trees. The caterpillars are often spotted in yards and parks where hickory or walnut trees are planted as ornamentals.

seasonality.spring: Adult moths emerge and mate in late spring. Fresh caterpillars begin appearing on host trees as tiny, less hairy versions of their mature selves.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for spotting the distinctive fuzzy caterpillars as they grow larger and more noticeable through mid to late summer. Adults are active at night, coming to porch lights.
seasonality.fall: Mature caterpillars become most visible in early fall as they finish feeding and search for pupation sites. They may wander considerable distances from their host trees.
seasonality.winter: Pupae overwinter in leaf litter or soil. No visible activity above ground during the cold months.

funFact: Despite decades of anecdotal reports claiming these caterpillars are venomous and can cause serious reactions, scientists have never actually found any venom in them – the skin irritation some people experience is simply from the mechanical irritation of the hairs, like getting a tiny splinter, not from any toxic chemicals!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the Spotted Tussock Moth caterpillar, which is also white and fuzzy but has yellow or orange spots along its back. Remember: Hickory Tussock = pure white body with black tufts, Spotted Tussock = white body with colorful spots.
contextualKnowledge: This species is also called the Hickory Tiger Moth, which can be confusing since the adult doesn't look much like other tiger moths with their bright warning colors. The "tiger moth" name refers to the family classification rather than the appearance – many tiger moth caterpillars are fuzzy and potentially irritating as a defense mechanism.
compareHints: The Hickory Tussock Moth is distinguished from its close relative, the Spotted Tussock Moth, primarily by the caterpillar stage – Hickory Tussock caterpillars are pure white with black hair tufts, while Spotted Tussock caterpillars have distinctive yellow, orange, or red spots along their white bodies. The adult moths of both species are similarly pale and spotted, making caterpillar identification the most reliable method.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Spotted Tussock Moth differs from its closest relative, the Hickory Tussock Moth, primarily in the caterpillar stage - Spotted Tussock larvae have distinctive black ends with a yellow-orange middle, while Hickory Tussock larvae are predominantly white with black spots scattered across their entire body.
